@@74314770 <h> Art Wrap : Four Exhibitions To See in Melbourne in April <p> One of Australia 's most iconic artists searches for paradise , a refreshing take on Melbourne 's greatest art collection , and some of Brunswick 's best galleries up the uber-cool art stakes . In partnership with Campari , here 's what to check out this month . <p> During the lockdowns of 2020 and 2021 , mums might have become familiar with the repetitive ' mummummumummummummum 's as they were constantly nagged and pulled in every direction . Eliza Hutchison is an established photographer whose work focuses on the biographical nature of photography , and her life as a mum . In her latest solo exhibition , we see a self-portrait of the Melbourne-based artist , though not in the traditional sense . As Hutchison explains , these latest works are a " generative visual biography " . <p> Four large-scale , inkjet prints on vinyl are hung side by side . Each depicts a digital collage of multiple computer screens , text message extracts and images from the youth climate change marches in Victoria in 2019 . Some of the imagery is quite pretty @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and old-school computer-style blocks of colour for example . At other times we catch a glimpse of deeply personal , everyday happenings , such as an image of a girl with her head buried in her hands . You might catch yourself trying to make sense of what you see , a hint at our everyday experience in a world saturated with digital images . <p> For decades , museums around the world have been teasing out alternative narratives in their permanent collections . The NGV recently opened Queer : Stories from the NGV Collection . This exhibition of artworks exclusively from the NGV collection has been years in the making , and involved curators consulting with LGBTQ+ and queer organisations and community members as part of the exhibition development process . <p> The resulting exhibition features approximately 400 artworks from antiquity to the present day . Highlights include Zanele Muholi 's mesmerising , black and white photograph of herself adorned with a glistening rope -- a comment on issues of gender politics , stereotypes of African women and race . Another is the flamboyant , floral satin dress by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ( c. 1988 ) . It is quintessentially Leigh -- the dress engulfs the model 's head ( complete with cut-outs for eyes and mouth ) and the look is completed with a black Kaiser helmet . Queer is a timely pick-me-up presenting the NGV Collection . <p> Almost 40 years ago , Melbourne-based artists Janet Burchill and Jennifer McCamley formed an artistic partnership . They 've been creating together ever since , with works spanning painting , sculpture , installation and film . Many of their works are a commentary on the history of art , design and culture , and they realise this interest by appropriating the imagery , language and mediums of their subject matter . <p> In their latest solo exhibition at Neon Parc , their subject is the French philosopher , mystic and political activist Simone Weil ( 1909-1943 ) , who in her short life wore many guises -- Marxist , Catholic , mystic -- to name a few . The artworks in the exhibition are comprised of identical screen prints on canvas , based on a single degraded image of Weil with her @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ image is printed on a Warhol-like , brightly coloured background , and accompanied by a word in all-caps which is synonymous with Weil 's thinking , such as " force " , " thing " , " prestige " and " attention " . Appearing side by side , the 12 artworks look like uncanny mug shots or post-mortem photographs . They 're unsettling , but intriguing at the same time . <p> Sidney Nolan is a common character of the Heide Museum of Modern Art repertoire , having lived at Heide in the 1940s , where he famously painted many of his Kelly works on the kitchen table . This exhibition delves into his lifelong pursuit of " something more " -- his journey of self-hood and his relationship to the places which he inhabited . <p> Arabian Tree , 1943 depicts a Garden of Eden with a man and a woman perched high up in tree -- the colours are lively , exuberant even -- perhaps reflection on his then-infatuation with Sunday Reed . Another work which plays perfectly into the thematic of the exhibition is Bird , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Reed 's sister in-law , Cynthia , and travelled to central Australia , Nolan depicts an imaginary , solitary bird high above a flat , desert-like landscape . For those who are unacquainted with Nolan 's work , a couple of the museum 's most iconic Kellys have also been included in the heavenly mix .

@@74318778 <p> Carolyn Butler-Madden ( main photo ) is the author of For Love &amp; Money and founder of The Cause Effect . In this guest post , Butler-Madden says brands can no longer ignore their social purpose responsibilities and offers her five reasons why ... <p> COVID-19 forced unimagined changes to our lifestyles and accelerated the adoption of new , more flexible ways of working . It also accelerated the movement of social purpose-led business ; driven by a recognition that governments alone , can not solve society 's most pressing challenges . While the pandemic hastened the pace of change , this movement was already underway pre-pandemic . To understand why business leaders can not afford to ignore the demand for businesses to adopt a social purpose , we need to examine the drivers behind it . There are five key drivers inspiring the social purpose movement : <p> Driver #1 : Society needs it <p> Society is facing enormous challenges , impacting people globally and exposing deep societal needs . We see the impact of climate change and COVID-19 continues to wreak havoc . The Russian attack on Ukraine has created a refugee crisis of enormous consequences @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of income inequality expose deep inequities not just between nations , but also within nations . These are large issues needing solutions , but there are many more . Businesses seeking to identify needs that they can serve do n't need to look far . A great source of reference to understand these issues is the Global Goals . These seventeen goals define society 's most critical challenges . The opportunity for business is to innovate to develop ways to serve them profitably . <h> Driver #2 : Societal leadership is now a core expectation of business <p> With governments proving themselves incapable of moving us towards a path of sustainability and equity , people are now looking to business for leadership . The 2022 Edelman Trust Barometer reveals that business is the only trusted institution , while NGO 's , Government and Media fall into neutral Trust territory . Crucially , societal leadership is now seen as a core business function amongst all stakeholders -- consumers , employees and investors . <h> Driver #3 : Businesses need to build trust <p> The expanded mandate of business to make a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change , provides businesses with an opportunity to build trust . Trust gains since the pandemic suggest that the public responded positively to the many positive stories of actions by business to roll their sleeves up to help . Businesses that adopt societal leadership as a strategic imperative will continue to build trust from employees , consumers and investors and secure the benefits that come with it . <h> Driver #4 : Meaningful work benefits everyone <p> In Australia 's first Meaningful Work Survey , Leadership , Culture and Purpose ranked as the most important contributors to meaningful work . Unsurprisingly , these are all intrinsically interlinked . Now consider what happens when people are engaged in meaningful work , driven by the pride they feel in working for a company with true leadership , a positive culture and engaged in work delivering meaningful impact to society . Employees feel a sense of fulfilment and self-worth , becoming emotionally invested in their work . This creates a powerful ripple effect , reaching recipients of the social impact the business creates and beyond . A happy fulfilled employee impacts positively on @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the wider community . This positive energy benefits everyone , not just the individual engaged in meaningful work . <p> Driver #5 : It makes good business sense <p> There is a growing body of credible evidence that shows social purpose is a strong driver of business success . Purposeful businesses financially outperform their counterparts , because their people are more engaged , the organisations more agile and , because there are higher levels of trust and loyalty in purposeful companies , they are more resilient when the going gets tough . <p> Social purpose is not just a passing trend , it is now the expectation of every business . <h> Latest News <p> InMobi , a leading provider of content , monetisation , and marketing technologies that help businesses fuel growth , today announced a partnership with Anzu.io , the world 's most advanced in-game advertising solution . @@74318811 <h> A film that humanises carbon ? Call me old-fashioned , but it feels counter-productive <p> This Australia-Canada co-production , the first under a new pact between the ABC and the CBC , has everything it needs to succeed : high production values , spectacular locations , a talented team with a passionate purpose , and what looks like a reasonable budget . On its own terms , it 's beautifully done . <p> The question is , what are those terms ? It 's an attempt to reimagine the story of carbon , a science-based repositioning of the world 's greatest building block so that we can all understand its importance . Thus , we have astro-physicists like Neil deGrasse Tyson and Tamara Davis explaining we are all carbon-based life forms , and British geologist Martin van Kranendonk showing us the origins of life itself in the stromatolites of the Pilbara . <p> We go down a coal mine in Mongolia and across a frozen arctic lake , where a scientist punches a hole in the ice and lights the methane that comes out . Another shows us how technology can return CO2 into the earth 's crust @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's clear from the various science lessons here that we came from outer space and we 're doing a good job of accelerating the return to an ashy uninhabitable planet . <p> The voice of Sarah Snook , soothing and svelte , whispers a personal narration . She plays Carbon itself , or rather , herself , because everyone the filmmakers talk to has adopted the conceit that carbon has a gender and it 's female . This has its dangers . <p> Ms Carbon explains that most of what we are doing to the planet is wrong -- and she will not forgive us . We will pay ; indeed , we 're already paying the price in climate change and extreme weather . <p> Loading <p> I did n't disagree with anything I heard here , but the manner of the message is problematic . By anthropomorphising carbon , the narration suggests a directive consciousness : we used to call that God , until Darwin gave us a different way of interpreting the natural world . <p> Scientist James Lovelock suggested in the 1970s that Gaia is a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we are the thing that needs correcting . The film never mentions Gaia , but by personalising carbon , giving Her a voice , they do n't need to . She 's there in every sentence . <p> Some will not object to this approach . The two directors -- Daniella Ortega in Australia and Niobe Thompson in Canada -- have assembled some great explainers . Who cares if they 've all been asked to call carbon " she " , and speak as if carbon has a conscious purpose . Call me old-fashioned , but I do . It took thousands of years of scientific work to free us from the idea that a greater consciousness was directing nature . Resurrecting that idea -- even just as metaphor -- is counter-productive if you want people to take responsibility for the world .

@@74321505 <h> When is a weather term clear and accurate ? When is it overblown ? And what 's the forecast for terms we 'll be hearing more often ? <p> Chatting about the weather is not what it used to be . Once a time-honoured form of small talk with strangers , these days it can be a matter of life and death . <p> There 's no doubt climate change has made it so ; and the damage from severe weather is terrible , as we have seen with flooding on the east coast . But with talk of supersized weather events swirling around increasingly -- from super-cyclones to mega-droughts -- how much of what we hear about weather is scientifically accurate and how much is , well , hyperbole ? <p> " Scientists get a little bit twitchy when we talk about using proper terms to describe the weather , " says Mark Gibbs , an oceanographer and climate researcher from Queensland University of Technology , " but that 's because if you do n't , it makes it murky for everyone else . " There are three essential categories of weather terms , he says : @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ usually coined in media reports ) . <p> So , when is a weather term clear and accurate ? When is it overblown ? And what 's the forecast for terms we 'll be hearing more often ? <h> Is an atmospheric river a real thing ? <p> Yes . Atmospheric rivers are actually the name given to a very specific and increasingly common weather pattern . And they 're closer to home than you might realise -- a weather system of this type was responsible for a year 's worth of rain being dumped in just a few days on south-east Queensland and northern NSW in late February , causing widespread flooding from the Sunshine Coast all the way to Sydney . Above is satellite imagery showing water vapour moving across the country in an " atmospheric river " during the rain event in February . <p> Advertisement <p> The term was first used informally by scientists but then , having appeared in multiple articles in scientific journals , it found its way to scientific acceptance , Gibbs says -- because it actually made sense . Atmospheric rivers are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ travel from one area to another in the same way a river on the ground directs water from higher areas to lower ones . <p> Loading <p> During the recent flood-causing rains , the river flowed from the Coral Sea to south-east Queensland for three days , pouring 16 Sydney harbours ' worth of water on the region before slowly moving south to flood Lismore and other regional centres . Because the water was falling on river catchments and built-up populated areas at the same time , Brisbane , in particular , saw both river flooding and flash flooding simultaneously . " Riverine flooding " and " flash flooding " are scientific terms that do tend to be used correctly in reporting , but bear explaining . Riverine flooding is when a river breaks its banks , often inundating nearby homes and buildings , while flash flooding occurs when there is a sudden heavy downpour that causes significant water runoff . <p> Because an atmospheric river is still not a widely known weather pattern , some commentary on the rain event that led to the flooding was incorrectly referred to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A series of infrared aerial photos of Lismore in March shows trees picked out in red , water in blue.Credit:Chad Ajamian <h> What 's a rain bomb ? <p> " Every meteorologist I know hates this term , " Gibbs says . " <p> Advertisement <p> The term is often used to describe any sudden heavy downpour , but a search of the Bureau of Meteorology 's website turns up no hits for the phrase , and asks if you instead meant " rainbow " . <p> It was used extensively in the early reporting of the heavy rains earlier this year , but Nina Ridder , a climate researcher at the ARC Centre of Excellence for Climate Extremes at UNSW , says it does n't work as a metaphor . " The term ' rain bomb ' suggests a sudden sharp downpour but , of course , the event we saw earlier this year was a sustained event @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Pitt Town as heavy rains associated with an east coast low impact the Sydney basin.Credit:Dean Sewell <h> What 's an east coast low ? <p> This is a genuine meteorological term referring to any " intense low-pressure systems which occur , on average , several times each year off the eastern coast of Australia " , according to the Bureau of Meteorology ( which calls them ECLs for short ) . <p> A low-pressure system is an area where the atmospheric pressure is lower than the surrounding areas . This causes air to rush in and swirl around in the centre , where air currents from different directions meet . It also draws in water vapour from the surrounding area , which then condenses into rain . <p> Basically , an area with high atmospheric pressure will usually have clear skies while low pressure equals rain and storms , and strong low-pressure systems develop into cyclones . <p> Advertisement <p> Loading <p> Crucially , east coast lows are not tropical cyclones , which the bureau distinguishes as a more intense storm system with higher winds . However , an east @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ over 100km/h as well as heavy rainfall . " It 's a very strong low-pressure system but not as strong as a tropical cyclone , " Ridder says . <p> " On the other hand , every time it rains it is not an east coast low , it 's a low-pressure system . East coast low is referring to a very specific set of weather conditions . " <h> Why are we hearing about hybrid cyclones ? <p> This is another scientific term used by meteorologists to refer to a cyclone with characteristics of both " warm " cyclones and " cold " cyclones . <p> A warm -- or " warm core " -- cyclone is what we would recognise as a tropical cyclone , one of its key features being that it is warmer than air surrounding it . A cold cyclone is created when different levels of the atmosphere have different temperatures , causing air to swirl around in a way that looks very similar to a warm cyclone . <p> The difference mostly matters to climatologists . Whether you 're in the middle of warm @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : a really big , nasty storm . <p> Advertisement <p> But the types of storms that are forming , and where , can give climatologists clues as to how the weather is changing as the climate shifts . Most storm cells use up their energy quickly ( think of a typical summer afternoon storm , which passes in less than half an hour ) but supercells have an internal feedback loop where they can spew out hail , rain and lightning for much longer , potentially causing far more damage . <p> And because they can drop a lot of water on an area for a sustained period they also come with a high risk of flash flooding -- although unlike an atmospheric river , they are self-contained and are n't drawing their moisture from a long way away . <p> Advertisement <p> Gibbs says because the term supercell sounds dramatic it is often used ( inaccurately ) to describe any large storm . There have been some high-profile examples in recent years , with temperatures dropping well below zero . In February 2021 , for instance , a polar vortex pushed cold air as far south as Texas , with more than 200 deaths both directly and indirectly attributed to the cold . A similar weather pattern in 2019 caused fewer deaths but was also felt over most of North America . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ because Australia is much closer to the equator than the landmasses of the Northern Hemisphere , it rarely affects us . <p> " There are differences in the weather patterns , too , because Antarctica is a land mass while the North Pole is just frozen ocean , so the air moves differently , " she says . <p> Antarctica -- the driest , windiest , coldest and iciest continent -- blocks wind from flowing as freely as it does at the North Pole , and therefore any vortex that might build in the south will be smaller . <h> What was The Duck ? <p> Believe it or not , this term is actually scientific , although it started its life at the other end of the weather-term spectrum , coined by commentators to refer to an unusual storm system in the Tasman Sea in 2001 , which had some features of a cyclone but was considered to have formed too far south to be classified that way . <p> That led reporters and , eventually , scientists to call it The Duck or even " Donald " in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ like a duck and quacks like a duck , it 's probably a duck " . " <p> Loading <p> Gibbs says today The Duck would be referred to as a hybrid cyclone . <p> Meanwhile , meteorologists do use the term " events " in relation to weather that is out of the ordinary . And it 's why investors in the current proxy voting season , in which shareholders vote on how their companies are run , are pushing companies to rethink packaging , building on successes of the past . <p> " Already , proxy voting has had an impact on the way companies reduce reliance on plastic packaging , " says Conrad MacKerron , senior vice president at As You Sow , an investor advocacy firm . " Some of the memorable things that we did several years ago are still notable . In 2018 , before this issue was quite as prominent as it is now , we got a commitment from McDonald's(MCD) to stop using polystyrene cups in their global system . In 2020 , Starbucks agreed to begin the process of moving towards eliminating single use coffee cups , another @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ microplastics get inside us ? Oftentimes , via the food we eat . Research in The Journal of Food Science found that humans ingest microplastics , some of it from the containers in which our food is stored or in which it arrives . A Harvard Health report finds that certain chemicals in plastic can leach out and into the food and beverages we eat , and some of these chemicals have been linked to health problems such as metabolic disorders ( including obesity ) and reduced fertility . <p> A possible solution would be to use less of the dangerous packaging materials and more of the safer and more sustainable ones . The problem is , this costs money , and companies are unlikely to make changes that will cost , unless they have to . Take Amazon.com ( AMZN ) and its packaging , for example . " The blue and white flexible packages with bubble wrap that Amazon uses to deliver its products to your door ? They are not recyclable , unfortunately . That 's a huge problem . The company has phased them out in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to . This shows that phasing out of these products can be done , it 's just a matter of willingness to do it in places where it 's not actually being forced to buy government policy , " says Conrad MacKerron , senior vice president at As You Sow . <p> So how can we get companies to change ? The proxy process plays a huge part in that . Similarly , the United Kingdom levied tax from 2022 on plastic packaging with less than 30% recycled materials . <p> " These requirements may increase costs for food companies in the short term because sustainable materials often carry a cost premium compared to cheap virgin plastic . Still , companies that adapt early may be best positioned to work collaboratively with existing suppliers , secure a stable supply of new materials , and gradually redesign their products and processes . In doing so , they may also be able to spread costs over time , while capitalizing on consumer awareness and brand recognition . " <p> Dr Jill Sheppard , a political researcher at the Australian National University agreed . <p> " We 've seen a lot in recent years how much government trust has eroded , and if a local member is considered to be tied up in that the electorate could be responding to that , " she said . <p> In the Victorian electorates of Corio and Corangamite , both within the greater Geelong region and held by Labor MPs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by 23.5 per cent and 20.2 per cent respectively since the 2019 election . <p> In Hunter , the NSW marginal seat currently held by outspoken Labor MP Joel Fitzgibbon , the issue grew by 21.8 per cent . <p> Dr Sheppard called these jumps " unprecedented " . <p> " There 's an anger that we have n't seen before in some electorates , " she said . <p> " Covid has shifted how we see government . @@90000068 <p> It 's more than a quarter of a century since a string of seats in western Sydney switched from red to blue and gave rise to a new type of voter : Howard 's battlers . <p> The urban electorates of Lindsay , Macarthur and Macquarie were emblematic of the shift . John Howard snatched all three from Labor with double-digit swings at the 1996 federal election , and they stuck with him for a decade . <p> John Howard and Jackie Kelly , the former Liberal member for Lindsay , attend a function in the electorate in 1996 . Credit:Robert Pearce <p> The Howard battler tag was an attempt to describe those won over by Howard 's brand of politics despite having attributes normally associated with Labor voters . They typically had a mortgage and worked in blue-collar jobs . They were concerned about interest rates , suspicious of high migration levels , worried about terrorism and often held socially conservative views . <p> Attention on Howard 's battlers dwindled after the defeat of the Howard government in 2007 and the Liberal 's electoral dominance of Sydney 's western fringe weakened . In 2016 Labor won back @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fringe -- Lindsay , Macarthur and Macquarie . <p> But Stewart Jackson , a specialist in Australian politics at Sydney University , says Howard 's battlers have not gone away . <p> " They are still there , " Dr Jackson says . " And they are quite possibly going to stick with the Coalition at the moment because interest rates are so low . " <p> Man of the people : John Howard on the campaign trail.Credit:Simon O'Dwyer <p> The seat perhaps most closely associated with Howard 's battlers is Lindsay , centred on Penrith in Sydney 's far west . The incumbent , Liberal Melissa McIntosh , was born there and worked for Howard as a junior press secretary in the late 1990s , so is familiar with the battler stereotype . <p> " Mr Howard himself called Lindsay a microcosm of the Australian community : families , retired people , small businesses and this amazing community spirit , " she says . That influx , driven by overseas migration , has redrawn electoral boundaries and altered the demographic character of many districts . <p> In 2001 , around 25 per cent of the population of Campbelltown council area ( within Macarthur ) were born overseas but by 2016 that had jumped to 38 per cent . " <p> Loading <p> But while the community is relatively new , some of their key concerns date back decades . <p> " Transportation options to the city are the most important thing , " says Hassan . The share of workers in the region employed in the service sector has grown steadily and there are higher levels of educational attainment . And what are the major issues that will divide voters and parties ? <p> Credit : <h> Who 's more popular at the moment ? <p> Exclusive polling for The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age , conducted by research company Resolve Strategic , shows that while voters liked Treasurer Josh Frydenberg 's budget , they did n't like it enough to vote Morrison their preferred prime minister . The polling has Albanese as preferred for the top job -- by 1 per cent . <h> What 's the caretaker period ? <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ member of parliament who will represent their local area . Now that the election has been called , the House of Representatives has been dissolved , and all 151 seats are up for grabs . The party or coalition that commands a majority of seats will then form the government . ( A half Senate election will also be held on election day , when 40 seats will be voted on -- half of the 72 " original " Senate seats plus two seats each for the Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory . ) <p> The caretaker period begins at the time the House is dissolved and continues until there is a clear election result . During an election campaign , government decisions need to continue until a new one is elected and so , by convention , the existing government acts as a " caretaker " to address important administrative and business duties . <p> Loading <p> Caretaker conventions say the government should avoid making major policy decisions , significant appointments or entering into major contracts or undertakings , including international negotiations and engagements . The reason the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is not committed to major policy decisions by a previous government . Ministers will often seek to clear the decks in the lead-up to an election . For example , the government has made more than 130 appointments to official jobs since March 21 . <p> Once the House of Representatives has been dissolved , writs must be issued within 10 days , but usually are much sooner . A writ is a document commanding an electoral officer to hold an election , and contains dates for the close of rolls , the close of nominations , the polling day and the return of the writs . The Governor-General issues writs for the House of Representatives election and the territories for Senate elections , and the state governors issue writs for the states ' Senate elections . <p> Advertisement <h> What are the key dates ? <p> Election day is on Saturday , May 21 and polling booths will be open between 8am and 6pm . Polling places are usually located in local schools , church halls or public buildings . <p> It is compulsory for all Australians over the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ n't already you can register to vote here . You must be correctly enrolled by 8pm on Monday , April 18 . <p> Early voting starts between 21 and 33 days following the issue of writs . If you live overseas or know that you wo n't be able to make it to a polling place on election day , you can vote early . There are a range of options for early voting , which include postal voting and in-person early voting . @@90020098 <p> Strap in for what promises to be one of the more nasty election campaigns , in which the characters of Prime Minister Scott Morrison and Opposition leader Anthony Albanese will be the main game . <p> At the previous two elections , in 2016 and 2019 , the campaigns were fought predominantly over issues of policy . <p> In 2019 for example , the government launched the campaign on a budget that was brought forward and contained tax cuts and promises of a return to surplus . <p> Labor entered the fray with a raft of tax policies -- too many , as it turned out -- focused on negative gearing , trusts , capital gains tax and franking credits , with the ultimate aim of outspending the government on health and education while balancing the budget . <p> In 2016 and 2019 climate change was a big subject of debate , as were the superannuation tax changes the government took to the 2016 election . <p> This time , there will be little of this substance . While the economy will feature large as it always does , fiscal discipline has diminished thanks to the pandemic , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ spend more than the government on " quality " measures is now a virtue . <h> Climate policy neutralised <p> The climate wars have been largely neutralised , as evidenced by Labor being able to release a policy with a 43 per cent emissions reduction target by 2030 , and a carbon price on heavy emitters to help achieve it , all of which has sunk without trace . <p> That is because the government , under Morrison 's leadership and cognisant of the capital markets and mugged by the political reality , has steered the Coalition away from coal towards a clean energy future firmed by gas along the way . <p> Climate change is a key issue of voter concern that straddles the political divide , and the Coalition 's poor record over the past decade and a half has left it exposed to challenges by independents in key inner-city seats , once deemed safe . <p> Scott Morrison visited Snowy 2.0 on December 3 as Labor announced its climate policy . Alex Ellinghausen <p> On the other side , Labor has jettisoned the entire policy agenda it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ target approach to win government . As recently as a week ago , it got rid of the last remaining tax proposal -- that to broaden the tax treatment of trusts . <p> Albanese has rolled out policies on energy security , the NBN , childcare , manufacturing , aged care and housing . None is particularly controversial or spectacular . Few voters would be able to recall any of them , but they still enable the Labor leader to proclaim he is not a policy-free zone . <h> Character a drag <p> Labor has made no secret for the past two-and-a-half years that its best shot at winning is to tear down Morrison 's character by driving perceptions he is a liar and a fraud . <p> At dress-rehearsal campaign rally in western Sydney late last year , Deputy Labor leader Richard Marles called the prime minister a liar 18 times in his warm-up speech . Marles was at it again on Insiders on Sunday morning as Morrison made his way to Government House , calling him a liar three times in one sentence . <p> In addition , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ COVID-19 pandemic to portray Morrison as incompetent , while giving no credit for things the government got right . <p> This concerted attack , helped by some friendly fire from within , the PM 's own mishandling of the Brittany Higgins allegations , and lingering memories of his trip to Hawaii in late 2019 as the country burned , has created a situation where Morrison 's personal unpopularity is a big drag on the government 's attempt to win a fourth term . <p> Aiming to be just the fourth Labor leader to win from Opposition since World War II , Albanese vowed to restore decency , responsibility and integrity to politics . <p> Advertisement <p> " I ca n't stand here today and promise you that I 'll get everything right , " he said . " But I can promise you if I get something wrong , I 'll own up to it , " he said . <p> " I may not always be the smoothest talker , but I can promise you I 'll always tell it straight . " <p> Morrison urged voters to put @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unravel Albanese -- as it did Bill Shorten in 2019 -- when he is scrutinised like never before . <p> " Elections are serious things . As the Australian people know , they know it 's not a reality show , it 's not based on who they like or do n't like , " he said . <p> " They know it 's about the economy they will live in as a result of the decisions that are taken by their government . <p> " Our government has shown that we 've been able to produce a stronger economy in the midst of the worst economic challenge and health crisis we 've seen in 100 years on health and 70 years when it comes to the economy . " <p> The South Australian election last month showed there is to be no reward for the handling of the pandemic . The British dumped Winston Churchill before World War II ended , and the stratospheric poll ratings Morrison and the premiers enjoyed during the worst pandemic in 100 years have gone , except in Western Australia . <h> Coalition ca @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ after taking all this into account , the Coalition is not dead yet . <p> Four major opinion polls just before the campaign -- AFR/Ipsos , Newspoll , Essential Research and the Resolve Political Monitor -- were all similar in terms of the starting point for the key players . <p> Labor 's primary vote lead is more a rejection of Morrison than an embrace of Albanese . Louie Douvis <p> The Coalition 's primary vote ranged from 34 per cent ( with undecided voters removed ) in the Resolve and Ipsos polls , to 37 per cent in the Essential poll . That three-percentage point range is pretty much within the margin of error . <p> Labor 's vote ranged from 39 per cent in Ipsos ( undecideds removed ) to 36 per cent in Essential . Again , a three-point range . <p> The rule of thumb is a minimum primary vote of 40 per cent is needed to win government . <p> As the election nears , the national polling numbers become less relevant , and it is , as a Coalition strategist pointed out , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the tracking polling each party conducts almost daily on the 20 or so seats that will decide the election . <p> The Coalition starts the campaign within the bare minium 76 seats and Labor 69 . There are six crossbenchers . A hung parliament for either party can not be ruled out . <p> For Morrison , it will be a localised campaign designed to sandbag seats at risk and to try and pinch a few off Labor to mitigate inevitable losses . <p> Advertisement <p> Ultimately , the government can not afford to go backwards on a net basis by even one seat . <p> But the polls show that while the voters have turned way from Morrison and the government , they have yet to flock to Labor and Albanese . <p> Labor 's primary vote , while higher than that of the government , does not have a four in front of it and Labor 's poll lead is more a rejection of Morrison than an embrace of Albanese . <p> The AFR/Ipsos poll , for example , found 30 per cent of voters approved of Albanese @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tie . <p> But a large 38 per cent had no view . @@90020107 <h> Explainer : The seats that will decide the election ( and why ) <p> To form government , a political party needs to win the majority of the 151 seats in the House of Representatives . <p> Some of those seats are considered safe , where the representative voted in at the last election is so popular that they are a shoo-in for re-election , or where a community has a strong political leaning in one direction . But there are a number of electorates across the country that are deemed at risk of changing political hands -- and they could win or lose the government an election . <p> Many of these seats are marginal , which the Australian Electoral Commission defines as ones held by a margin of under 6 per cent ( where the winning party beat their closest opponent by less than 6 per cent of the vote at the last election after accounting for preferences ) . <p> " Safe seats " are defined as those with a margin of between 6 per cent and 10 per cent , and " very safe seats " are those with margins above 10 per cent @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the more competitive the race between the candidates in that electorate at the next election is deemed to be . <p> As a result , those marginal seats -- where only 6 per cent of voters ( or less ) need to be convinced to vote differently in order for the electorates to change hands -- tend to be a key focus of the major political parties in the lead up to the election . <p> But not all the seats to watch are marginal . There are a number of safe Liberal seats being challenged by well-educated , well-connected and well-funded businesswomen who are frustrated that not enough is being done by the current government , particularly when it comes to climate action , and they are building momentum within their electorates . <p> There are also a number of popular MPs who are retiring from politics , which could allow for other political parties and their candidates to get their foot in the door . <p> These are the key seats across the country that could decide the election . <p> Advertisement <h> What are the seats to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for Scott Morrison if he is to lead the government to a come-from-behind victory . <p> Twelve months ago , the Coalition had identified up to 10 Labor-held seats as targets to offsetting losses elsewhere , although the chance of winning a swag have faded along with the PM 's poll numbers . <h> Gilmore <p> Where : Gilmore covers several towns along the NSW South Coast from Kiama in the north to Tuross Head down south as well as Batemans Bay , Berry , Gerroa and Ulladulla . <p> Why : The government 's best chance of a gain is Gilmore , where former state minister Andrew Constance is up against first-term Labor MP Fiona Phillips . <p> Phillips defeated Liberal Party candidate Warren Mundine in 2019 , after he was parachuted into the seat . @@90020111 <p> The prospect of the eighth successive federal election without either party offering any serious economic reform is a wake-up call for business . <p> The leading business lobby group , the Business Council of Australia , needs to rethink its approach to political engagement . It is time to abandon the failed approach of dogged advocacy , which comes across to many observers as whinging . <p> Tax reform and industrial relations reform will never get off the ground until business does its fair share of work to build a constituency for change . <p> Over the past decade , the Liberals , the Nationals and Labor have become sick of business telling them the country needs reform only to find that when a political battle ensues , business just disappears . <p> The pathway for reform involves coming to the government with detailed policy ideas that can then be scrutinised from the point of view of whether they are truly in the national interest and based on hard evidence . <p> Advertisement <p> Business has to build a constituency for change and once that has happened it should come to the government with proof it can work @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ comes to this task with a distinct advantage . The 100 or so companies that are members of the BCA employ more than 1 million people . Chief executives of these companies have the power to build momentum for nation-building ideas . <p> Far-sighted companies can pass on to government the lessons learned from the millions of day-to-day interactions they have with the domestic and global economy . <p> Business is at the forefront of the mega-trends changing society including dealing with the convergence of technology , entertainment , finance and data analytics . <p> CEOs and boards of directors know we are heading into several decades of disruption that will have winners and losers . Australia can be a winner in a world where success is about intellectual property and not exporting commodities to China . <h> Big policy ideas <p> Advertisement <p> Business can champion the big policy ideas that should flow from dispassionate analysis of the winning strategies , which are capital-light and rely on a highly skilled and flexible workforce . Winning business models churn profits into research and development instead of paying out 70 per @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on to politicians the lessons learned from facing up to the challenges posed by the increasing power of hyperscale cloud computing operators such as Amazon , Microsoft and Google . <p> For example , there are clearly sovereign risks from our big four banks having about 80 per cent of their cloud storage with two companies . <p> A change in the business lobby 's strategy for engagement with government would be a tacit recognition that the political class no longer has the appetite for the extremely hard work involved in economic reform . <p> The last truly reform-driven election was John Howard in 1998 , which asked for a mandate to introduce the goods and services tax ( GST ) . <p> Both sides of politics appear to have lost sight of former prime minister Paul Keating 's mantra that a politician 's job is to explain the future to a fearful and sceptical electorate . <p> Advertisement <p> Prime Minister Scott Morrison 's key message at the weekend was the opposite of this . He essentially said stick with me for a risk-averse , business-as-usual approach . Opposition @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ advocacy to ideas <p> The economic reforms needed to put Australia on a better path have been well-rehearsed and , in most cases , have been well articulated in study after study . Tax reform is a case in point . <p> The Australian Financial Review 's idea that the next government conduct a rapid-fire review of the country 's tax settings is a good one . <p> It could explore the implications and second-order impacts of a higher GST and the opportunity it presents to lower income taxes for lower tax bands . A review could examine the implications of ending the free rides from negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts . <p> The review could ride off the back of the states which favour a move from stamp duty to broad-based land taxes that capture the super profits earned by Sydney harbourside house flippers . Also , it could explore the benefits from implementing the world-leading innovation incentives found in Israel . <p> Advertisement <p> Business could back this Financial Review taxation probe with unique research analysing customer data . This could help policymakers understand how to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Energy is another obvious area crying out for policy reform . It would benefit from business being at the vanguard of exploring new ways of looking at carbon reduction strategies . <p> Ideas worth exploring include increased government investment in a smart energy grid to accommodate more renewables , and intervention in the gas market on the eastern seaboard to secure lower domestic gas prices . <p> It is obvious we need to put a price on carbon to stimulate private spending on energy efficiency and electric cars . Business research into the upside from such a change would not only help frame the debate , but it could also reinforce the good sense in rational decision-making . <p> A switch from advocacy to ideas by the business lobby could allow realistic exploration of truly radical propositions that can never be debated as part of the current political process . <p> A good case in point is the idea pushed by Microsoft founder Bill Gates for the use of small modular nuclear reactors . There are about 18 SMRs operating in the world . <p> Advertisement <p> It is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ largest uranium resources in the world and exports the raw materials for nuclear power but has ruled out being a beneficiary of the ore . <p> Understanding the economics of controversial options such as nuclear power make sense when the government settings arguably have Australia on the path towards a worst-case scenario on climate change with possible catastrophic consequences . <p> Other radical ideas that could be floated and explored by business , or business-funded think tanks , are a review of the federation and the possibility of removing a layer of government . That could be part of national simplification and alignment of all administration between states . <p> The concept of business contributing to the national debate in a nonconfrontational way appears to underpin the funding of an independent inquiry into the COVID-19 pandemic . <p> The inquiry is led by former senior public servant Peter Shergold , who was secretary of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet from 2003 to 2008 . It is being funded by the Minderoo Foundation , Paul Ramsay Foundation and the John and Myriam Wylie Foundation . <p> Who knows , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can one day help a politician develop a reform agenda that resonates with Australians. 
@@90020116 <p> Labor is burnt from its big-target , tax-and-spend agenda in 2019 . It has dumped tax crackdowns on negative gearing , capital gains concessions , trusts and franking credits . <p> Labor now supports the Coalition 's stage three personal income tax cuts for higher earners , set to begin in July 2024 . <p> Advertisement <p> Albanese has stripped out any areas of major contention , while promising to spend more on childcare , aged care , TAFE and the energy grid . <p> A crackdown on multinational tax avoidance is Labor 's main revenue raiser , with details still to be outlined . <p> The budget deficit is forecast to remain entrenched at $40 billion to $80 billion a year over the next four years . Neither side is canvassing spending cuts or tax rises to narrow the gap . <p> The government says growing the economy will shrink debt as share of GDP , while Labor insists the quality of spending matters at least as much as the quantity and size of budget deficits . <p> Advertisement <p> Climate change and the great energy transition will lead to a major transformation of the Australian economy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 2050 net-zero emissions target , Labor 's 2030 emission reduction target of 43 per cent is more ambitious than the Coalition 's projection of 35 per cent , but is still short of the Business Council of Australia 's 46-50 per cent goal . <p> Labor has some semblance of a credible policy . The so-called safeguard mechanism will stop big firms polluting above business-as-usual levels and allow the trading of permits between companies . <p> The Coalition labels it a secret carbon tax , but the truth is neither side of politics is goading for a rerun of the climate wars at this election . <p> John Kehoe is Economics editor at Parliament House , Canberra . @@90020129 <h> Three balancing acts that just got harder <p> The COVID-19 pandemic shocked the global economy , countered by central banks with a massive increase in fiscal and monetary stimulus . The pandemic shocked globally integrated supply chains , resulting in inflation . <p> Somewhat surprisingly though , the pandemic has n't detracted from a focus on climate change , but has instead given more impetus on global efforts to decarbonise . <p> The war in Ukraine has made central banks ' task much harder to calibrate . Simon Letch <p> In response to this , three endeavours are now underway : central bankers are reversing course to target their policy efforts at containing inflation ; corporates are restructuring their supply chains to build in greater resiliency ; and -- on varying timeframes -- governments and companies are formulating strategies to achieve net zero carbon emissions . <p> Each endeavour is a difficult balancing act , and the conflict in Ukraine has just made each of them more difficult . <p> Central banks were already walking a tightrope by trying to figure out how to wind back the huge stimulus of the pandemic without derailing the global economic recovery @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ much harder to calibrate . <p> Advertisement <p> If central banks keep policy too loose , our expectation of inflation could become entrenched . Then , when growth eventually slows after the post-pandemic surge , we 're left with stagflation . <p> On the other hand , if central banks raise rates aggressively to get inflation expectations under control , they could tip the global economy into recession -- which is what it usually takes to get an inflation cycle under control . And , if they raise rates a lot and shrink central bank balance sheets , the loss of liquidity could prompt a repricing of assets . <h> Tangled supply chains <p> The second balancing act that has come to the fore is the deglobalisation of supply chains . <p> After decades of falling trade barriers , slick financial integration and easy logistics , supply chains became ever-more dispersed . But these three facilitating forces are now reversing , and the sanctions resulting from the conflict in Ukraine have shown how quickly those reversals can occur . <p> Accountability for the design of supply chains used to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ focus on efficiency . Now the chief risk officer wants a say , bringing a different set of priorities to bear . <p> Advertisement <p> If efficiency is no longer the sole focus of supply chains , then corporate costs will go up . Without wage increases and raw material imposts , this would be more manageable ; in a period of generalised inflation there are many difficult decisions to be made between shorter term cost of supply and longer-term security of supply . <h> Chasing net zero <p> The push to decarbonise is the third difficult balancing act . <p> On one hand , if energy shortages in Europe require more coal and gas , and fears over high energy prices slow down the energy transition , then the world is at risk of cumulative emissions being higher than the climate can withstand . The recent spike in energy prices , and impact on households , shows just how tightly balanced energy markets are . <p> But if we 're too fast turning off oil , gas and coal , paying for everyday energy needs will crowd out spending @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ petrol tank are taking a larger slice of people 's wallets , fewer people will be able to afford to put solar panels on their roof or buy electric cars . <p> Advertisement <p> Any further increase in energy prices that could be attributed to efforts to decarbonise , may see public support for decarbonisation falter . We saw this happen after the GFC , when people 's focus shifted from saving the planet to just getting by . <p> There are no simple answers and the world will muddle through to the least-worst outcomes . It would all be rather grim if we did n't have capitalism 's two superpowers of innovation and market pricing to rely on . <p> Kate Howitt is portfolio manager of the Fidelity Australian Opportunities Fund . <p> Kate Howitt is portfolio manager of the Fidelity Australian Opportunities Fund .

@@90039186 <h> Let 's use this election to raise the quality of the politics we get <p> This may be my 18th election as a journalist , but I confess I find the thought of a six-week campaign a bit daunting . Six weeks of unrelenting political argy-bargy ? <p> Still , it does afford the luxury of one column discussing how we approach elections , before we get down to the many economic challenges the new government will face : climate change , wage stagnation , unaffordable home ownership and wasteful spending on infrastructure , not to mention integrity in government . <p> In elections , it 's always tempting to vote for the devil you know -- a line pushed by all governments . But when you think about it , you see this notion is biased completely in favour of the incumbent . It seeks to shift the voter 's attention away from the government 's performance and play on our timidity . <p> What do you know about the other lot ? Not much . How do you know they wo n't be worse ? You do n't . But , then again , they could @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ devil-you-know rule , one side of politics would stay in power for ever . Not to me , it does n't . In my experience , the longer governments stay in power , the worse they get . They get lazy and complacent . They worry more about helping their friends and less about keeping the rest of us happy . <p> They develop a sense of entitlement . They think they own the place and it 's their own money they 're spending . They get more and more reluctant to be held accountable by nosy outsiders and more inclined to keep their failures buried deep . <p> And that 's just the deterioration in government . The side kept out of power for year after year also goes off . Fewer and fewer of their leading lights have ever been a minister . Which , of course , is all they were given . <p> It would n't be good for our governance if government changed hands every three or four years . @@90041065 <h> Pursuit home <h> Dengue-blocking mosquitoes here to stay <p> Mosquitoes carrying anti-viral bacteria show remarkable stability a decade since their release in field trials . New strains have now been developed to help future-proof dengue control <p> By Dr Perran Ross , University of Melbourne <p> Share selection to : <p> Dengue fever and other mosquito-borne diseases remain a massive threat to human health and wellbeing . Urbanisation and climate change are likely to increase this threat as established mosquitoes spread to new environments and gain a foothold . <p> Eradicating all disease-spreading mosquitoes is n't possible , but we might be able to do the next best thing . For the last decade , we 've been using bacteria called Wolbachia to reduce the ability of mosquitoes to spread the dengue virus . <h> WOLBACHIA TO THE RESCUE <p> Wolbachia lives inside the cells of about half of all insect species . The bacteria can have a variety of effects on their hosts , from providing essential nutrients to killing male offspring . When transferred to mosquitoes , the bacteria reduce the ability of many viruses to replicate inside the mosquito and be passed on to a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ levels in mosquito populations because it is passed from females to all their offspring . <p> Although males that carry Wolbachia ca n't pass the infection on , any female mosquitoes they mate with that lack Wolbachia wo n't produce offspring . This gives any unlucky mosquitoes that do n't have Wolbachia a big disadvantage . So by introducing dengue-blocking Wolbachia to the local mosquito population , most mosquitoes that survive are unlikely to pass on the dengue virus . <h> How long will Wolbachia releases be effective ? <p> For Wolbachia releases to be sustainable , it 's important that the bacterium remains at high levels in the mosquito population and provide ongoing protection against dengue . Our study published earlier this year in PLoS Pathogens finds remarkable long-term stability of Wolbachia . <p> We monitored mosquito populations a decade after the first release of Wolbachia in Australia and found that its effects on mosquitoes remained intact . Furthermore , there were no detectable changes in the genome of Wolbachia . <p> Our research suggests that Wolbachia is likely to be effective for a very long time , but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ A Wolbachia strain for every situation <p> We have developed new Wolbachia strains using a technique called microinjection , where Wolbachia is sucked out of an egg carrying the strain of interest and injected into a donor mosquito egg . If you 're lucky , the mosquito that hatches will pass on the Wolbachia to their offspring . <p> The wMel strain is being used widely in Wolbachia release programs , but it 's vulnerable to high temperatures . This means that Wolbachia could drop out of mosquito populations during the hotter parts of the year and might be unsuitable for release in some climates altogether . <p> Although Australian and Malaysian mosquitoes have distinct differences , the effects of Wolbachia were consistent in both groups . This provides confidence that Wolbachia releases will have similar outcomes in different mosquito populations , but it 's also important to consider the impact of local environmental conditions . <h> Beyond Wolbachia <p> Wolbachia is one of many types of bacteria that could be used to modify or control insect pests for our benefit . <p> Japanese encephalitis , Ross River virus and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ mosquitoes and all of them could potentially be controlled with Wolbachia release programs . @@90041076 <p> Australian foreign policy is characterised by the perpetual dilemma of grand strategy : aligning lofty aspirations ( shaping the Indo-Pacific ) with limited resources ( a population of 26 million and relative economic decline ) . If Australia is to meet its ambitions , it must better marshal all its national assets . To this end , the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade should develop a new policy capability to connect domestic policy agencies in Australia with those in the Indo-Pacific . <p> The provision of public goods is increasingly a domain for strategic competition . Those who can provide ways and means to address difficult challenges facing societies -- economic development , climate change , governance and health , to name a few -- can not only win favour , but also help spread and entrench norms . This is precisely why Australia , both independently and through groupings like the Quad , has made public goods like infrastructure and vaccines key elements of its regional engagement . <p> Shadow Foreign Minister Penny Wong recently said , ' Given the circumstances we face , we really need to deploy all aspects of state power : strategic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australia 's greatest assets is its sophisticated governance , underpinned by a well-resourced and highly qualified public sector . Australian federal , state and territory governments hold world-leading expertise in all aspects of social and economic policy . This public knowledge is supplemented by universities and think tanks . <p> Australia should see its domestic public policy infrastructure as a foreign policy asset . While DFAT , and other agencies , already fund capacity-building and technical assistance in the Indo-Pacific , much of this is ad hoc , limited to discrete projects , and often contingent on the initiative of individual diplomats . There are no mechanisms to track and leverage the influence this work generates . <p> The Australian Electoral Commission and the Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre show the significant value domestic agencies can add to foreign policy goals : boosting electoral transparency and combating illicit finance promote good governance and show Australia to be a constructive regional player . These examples are , however , the exception . Most domestic policy agencies at the federal and especially state and territory levels understandably have little capacity to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ more structured approach , facilitated by DFAT , is needed . Imagine , for example , investigators from the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption advising their regional counterparts . Or domestic violence policymakers in state and territory governments sharing their knowledge and experience to help protect women and girls throughout the region . Or Australian experts in environmental and natural resource management being better utilised in countries threatened by climate change . <p> Focusing on technical assistance , capacity-building and governance plays to Australia 's strengths . It also provides a more sustainable way of competing with malign actors that have deeper pockets . If the current imbroglio in Solomon Islands over a draft security agreement with China has taught Australia anything , it should be that investing in long-term governance should receive equal priority to direct financial support . <p> So , what could a domestic policy capacity in DFAT look like ? It would need to be a fully resourced division that 's well connected to federal and state bureaucracies , as well as to academics and think tanks . While based in Canberra , most of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and territory offices to be plugged into each jurisdiction 's capabilities . <p> The domestic policy division would serve three main purposes . First , it could provide a ' screening ' function to advise subnational government agencies against relationships with foreign counterparts that are contrary to their national interests , complementing the foreign arrangements scheme . As a recent ASPI report showed , ' paradiplomacy ' by subnational actors can contradict federal foreign policy . <p> Second , this policy area would generate connections between Australian and foreign governments in areas where links do n't already exist but would be advantageous . This dialogue could go both ways : sharing Australian policy expertise abroad while bringing international insights into domestic discourse . There 's a precedent here in the ' first movers ' group formed in 2020 on reopening after Covid-19 's first wave . Reciprocal policy dialogue would also encourage domestic agencies to take part . <p> In these exchanges , DFAT would provide the diplomatic legitimacy and connections allowing subject-matter expertise to be exchanged . The department could also help build international engagement capacity and ensure interactions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ this work would be opportunistic , DFAT could proactively canvass the needs of Indo-Pacific nations and identify complementary capabilities in the Australian system . DFAT should also have a dedicated budget to subsidise the participation of domestic agencies . <p> The domestic policy division 's third purpose would be to systematically track connections between Australian and foreign governments and leverage them for strategic advantage . This could also include the multilateral engagement in technical forums that other Commonwealth agencies have responsibility for , such as in health , infrastructure and industry . By auditing these links , Australia can access more points of influence , collate a deeper well of personal and institutional ties with other nations , better understand the pressure points for partner governments , and respond quickly in crises . <p> With the Labor opposition linking domestic resilience to international influence , while also promising to rebuild Australian diplomacy if it wins the election , DFAT should dream big . @@90142778 <h> Democracy is failing to tackle the climate crisis <p> The structures of democracy must change in order for the world to overcome crises such as climate change , writes Dr Helen Camakaris . <p> AS THE lead-up to the Federal election in Australia gathers steam , each major party is courting the public , almost exclusively focused on winning the numbers game . <p> Like most of us , politicians are swayed by emotive reasoning and suffer the many shortcomings of evolutionary mismatch ; they , therefore , tend to favour short-term interests , namely re-election , and the pursuit of status . <p> As always , the lynchpin of the Coalition 's electoral policy involves pork-barrelling in marginal electorates , targeting the hip pocket nerve with a short-term fistful of dollars ( or longer-term if you are wealthy and qualify for tax breaks ) and claiming superior financial management , even when there is scant evidence . <p> And rather than Basil Fawlty 's refrain , " do n't mention the war " , Morrison has capitalised on the zeitgeist of war as a plus for the Liberal Party . It 's more a case of " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Labor , meanwhile , is pursuing a sales pitch for improved aged care , an appropriate response to the Royal Commission 's 2021 recommendations , improved Medicare and cheaper child care . At least , they have a plan for tackling climate change , with their powering Australia policy , slated to reduce emissions by 43 per cent by 2030 and put us on track for net-zero by 2050 , in line with Australia 's Paris commitments , whilst boosting jobs in renewable energy . <p> In Australia , climate policy is a major problem , despite the fact that we are extremely vulnerable to the climate 's impacts . We face severe disruption with worsening droughts , floods , bushfires , heatwaves , rising sea levels , ocean acidification and cyclones . <p> Over the past two decades in Australia , the political rabble has deposed responsible leaders on both the left and right , fearing that the public is too unsophisticated to consider any issue not immediately evident as serving self-interest . <p> Current democracies ignore the fact that the majority of voters sit in the political centre @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Similarly , the rights of future citizens and people beyond our borders are routinely ignored . <p> At least two changes are necessary : firstly , we must move away from adversarial jousting between left- and right-wing ideologies , to seek meaningful representation and consensus ; and secondly , we must tap into the specialist knowledge necessary to comprehensively understand issues like climate change from all angles : scientific , social , psychological , political , economic and ethical . <p> As an interim measure , decisions on global , long-term issues like climate change ( and indeed , the nature of democracy itself ) , could be made by a government-sponsored independent council for the future that includes experts in science , economics , political theory , foreign policy , international law , psychology and ethics . <p> They could jointly design policy on solving climate change , which could then be put before the government or a citizens ' assembly for a conscience vote . <p> Climate policy would be at arm 's length from politics , much as happens with the Federal Reserve in the USA and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Making a controlled transition , without conflict , is the challenge for any substantive change in politics , but a council for the future would tick many boxes . <p> One possible strategy involves promising a council for the future as part of an election platform . The public is keen to see progress on " wicked problems " and could well support a party with a strategy that might allow us to secure a safe future for our children . <p> Dr Helen Camakaris is a retired research scientist and an Honorary Fellow at the University of Melbourne . You can follow her on Twitter : @helenmcama. 
@@90160573 <h> It will demand an iron will , but it 's not too late for Albanese to change track <p> One of the hardest lessons to learn in politics is that it is never too late to make a change . If you are the leader , or in the leader 's office , it can seem horribly hard to pull the cumbersome weight of campaign machinery from one rail onto the other -- but it can always be done . <p> By Wednesday , Anthony Albanese 's need to shift the focus of this campaign away from his mistakes was clear . Neither happened . <p> The past week reminded me of Peter Hartcher 's 2019 observation that Bill Shorten 's policy offerings were an IKEA flat-pack : you needed to assemble them yourself , while Morrison simply hammered economics . This campaign is different , built less around policy visions and more around destroying your opponent . But Labor is making the same mistake . Together , they looked terrible , and Albanese @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ But how can you determine the import of each for an actual Albanese government ? This depends entirely on speculation . Did his lack of clarity on immigration indicate a lack of commitment on boats or was this an absurd over-reading of a bland statement ? <p> Advertisement <p> You will have your own answers . The undeniable fact is that these speculative and unknowable aspects of the campaign have so far received far more attention and weight than empirically provable facts supporting what we already know . <p> Morrison , in his attacks right now , has two advantages . The first is that he has one clear attack . The second is that this attack plays to the media 's preference . The perverse difficulty for Labor is that the various government failings last week offered confirmation , not revelation . We knew about the Morrison government 's pork-barrelling , its problems with women , its ugly willingness to play politics with trans people 's lives -- and unfortunately @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on the novel and unknown . Why talk about tedious facts the voters more-or-less know when you can speculate endlessly about a mysterious future ? That is the chance Morrison has given political journalists with his talk about a " blank page " . It is not so different from the media 's decision in 2019 to focus on the unknown cost of Shorten 's climate policies rather than what was already known about a government that did not care about climate change . <p> Loading <p> That is part of the story . The rest is that Albanese brought this on himself . The mistakes were spontaneous , but their impact was in part the consequence of his earlier decision to adopt a small-target strategy . Until now , that decision had seemed cost-free . It was n't . A large policy offering , made months ago , would have told voters what Labor planned to do , reassuring them ; made them feel they knew who Albanese was , rendering campaign mistakes less important ; and , most obviously , given Albanese practice at being a target . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of its policies has left Albanese vulnerable to the government 's message he is negative . This may be what stopped Labor attacking as hard as it needed to last week . It is clearly caught between the many things it feels it should do : introduce Albanese , announce policy , attack hard but avoid seeming carping . <p> Loading <p> Only so much can be achieved by either side in the five weeks that remain . Morrison knows this : he ca n't fix the opinions people have of him , but he can direct their attention to speculation about his opponent . Similarly , Albanese can not now do everything that has been put off for three years . How does he meet inevitable speculation with fact , about his opponent and himself ? <p> Some sharp choices will be necessary : a discarding of superfluous elements . Campaigns often resist change , worried about the message of panic it might send . The truth is most people will not notice . It is never too late to shift strategy , and there is no shame in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Still , to make changes in the middle of a national campaign demands imagination , agility , self-belief and iron will . Whether Albanese has these we are about to find out .

@@90161029 <h> ' Race against time ' : Scientists ' desperate move to save rare frog <p> Tucked away in the alpine region of the Kosciuszko National Park , 80 frogs are settling into new homes as scientists race against the clock to protect these valuable animals from extinction . <p> The spotted tree frog is critically endangered in NSW , just one step away from being extinct , and is one of many species battling a range of threats , including diseases and changing climate . This year , the NSW government released 80 spotted tree frogs into Kosciuszko National Park after they were severely affected by the unprecedented 2019-20 summer bushfires . <p> The spotted tree frogs are enjoying their new home in the Kosciuszko National Park.Credit:Alex Pike <p> NSW Minister for Environment James Griffin said the species disappeared in the state in 2001 due to the chytrid fungus that almost wiped out the southern and northern corroboree frogs . Through work between the government 's Saving our Species program and the Amphibian Research Centre in Melbourne , the frogs have been given a second chance . <p> " In 2015 , our threatened species experts released spotted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and it 's estimated that there were between 250-300 frogs in the wild , " Griffin said . " Tragically , it 's estimated that only about 10 of those frogs survived the devastating 2019-20 bushfires . " <p> Department of Planning and Environment senior threatened species officer David Hunter said the fragile alpine ecosystem where the frogs lived was unique to NSW and Victoria and featured native wildlife found nowhere else on Earth . <p> " The spotted tree frog is fundamental to the maintenance of ecosystem health in the NSW upland rivers where it lives . It occupies many streams where they are the only frog species , and tadpoles of this species consume nutrients and algae in large numbers , " Hunter said . <p> " They are also food for other species such as snakes , birds , mammals and predatory invertebrates , playing an important role in the food web . " <p> Department of Planning and Environment senior threatened species officer Dave Hunter releases a spotted tree frog , which is only 6cm in length.Credit:Alex Pike <p> Only 12 populations of the spotted tree @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ north-western side of the Great Dividing Range , between the Central Highlands and Mt Kosciusko in NSW . <p> Advertisement <p> The Victorian Department of Land , Water and Planning said the species had disappeared from half of its known historic sites and was expected to become extinct without intervention . <p> The Australian Museum amphibian biologist and conservationist Dr Jodi Rowley said frogs played a vital part in the environment and were known as bioindicators , which are used to assess how healthy an ecosystem is . Without them , entire ecosystems can collapse . <p> The frogs have a very distinctive call used during mating season.Credit:Alex Pike <p> " They are the glue that sticks ecosystems together . In places where frogs have had dramatic declines there are nothing that steps up to fill that role , " she said . <p> " There are irreversible changes : the steams are full of algae because the tadpoles are n't there to eat it , animals that rely on frogs waste away . We need frogs . " <p> She added that the recent wet summer could create the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , with scientists planning to conduct field research in coming months to see how severely the species had been impacted . <p> Loading <p> One of the main threats facing frogs was the chytrid fungus , she said , but the additional pressures of introduced predators -- such as cats and foxes -- as well as bushfires , droughts and climate change were severely affecting the species . They are not the only animal struggling in a rapidly changing climate . <p> The latest NSW State of the Environment report found almost 20 animals and plants have been added to the threatened species list in the past three years . Modelling predicts that only 496 of the 991 terrestrial species listed as threatened are predicted to survive in 100 years ' time . <p> " It is a race against time , " Rowley said . " One of the major challenges with frog conservation is that we are struggling to get the information we need to make the best decisions . " <p> While there are projects that rely on the help of citizen scientists to document frog populations @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " We 're at a pivotal time in history which is terrifying and exciting : we have the ability and power to turn things around , " she said .

@@90178222 <p> It has never been easier to be green . Now more than ever , since the sustainability movement took hold of the development sector more than two decades ago , property owners are being financially snubbed for holding assets with low green credentials . <p> Lenders and investors are penalising the last generation of real estate offerings because they do not meet emission targets , are considered too costly to maintain or will be hard to sell . <p> Property owners using solar panels and batteries are increasingly selling excess energy back to the grid . Supplied <p> Insurers are following suit , factoring in climate change to deliver more fires , storms and floods when assessing the disaster resilience of older buildings . Since the end of the most recent lockdown , many commercial tenants have sought to relocate to green buildings as part of plans to entice staff back into the office . <p> So , some property owners , particularly of pre-2000 product , are facing more risks and responsibilities .
